problem: FundedNext runs its trading platform, payment rails, and CEx tooling (AgentPlatform, CEx Pulse) on a mix of on-prem-style VPS infrastructure and cloud services. The moment any workload touches a public cloud provider, the security perimeter you grew up trusting — a physical firewall at the edge of a data center — stops existing. A misconfigured S3-equivalent bucket, an overly permissive IAM role, or an exposed management console can leak trader KYC documents, payout data, or internal support tickets to the entire internet in seconds, with no firewall to stop it.

The business problem Cloud Security solves is: how do you protect data, identity, and workloads when the infrastructure is owned and operated by someone else, shared with thousands of other tenants, and reachable from anywhere by design? For a fintech like FundedNext, this isn't academic — a single leaked bucket of trader documents or an unrotated API key committed to a public repo can trigger regulatory exposure, reputational damage, and direct financial fraud.
Real-world trigger examples: public S3-style buckets, leaked cloud API keys in code, over- permissioned IAM roles, unpatched cloud VM images, unmonitored root/admin account logins.
concept: Cloud Security is the discipline of protecting data, identities, workloads, and configurations across cloud- hosted infrastructure using a Shared Responsibility Model. In this model, the cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP) secures the physical data centers, hypervisor, and core network — the security OF the cloud.

The customer (FundedNext) is responsible for everything they configure on top: IAM policies, network security groups, data encryption choices, OS patching on VMs, and application-level access control — security IN the cloud.

This is fundamentally different from on-prem security, where your team controls the whole stack. In cloud, most breaches are not the provider's fault — they are customer misconfiguration. Gartner has repeatedly stated that the vast majority of cloud security failures are the customer's, not the provider's, which is why this session sits directly after the Layer 6 detection/response stack you just finished: the same principles (least privilege, defense in depth, zero trust) apply here, just re-implemented as cloud- native controls instead of on-prem hardware.
Identity & Access Management (IAM) — who can do what, on which resource
Data protection — encryption at rest, in transit, and key management
Network security — VPCs, security groups, private endpoints
Configuration/posture management — finding and fixing misconfigurations (CSPM)
Workload protection — securing VMs, containers, and serverless functions
Logging, monitoring, and incident response in a cloud-native context
deep: Shared Responsibility Model by service type Service Model Provider Secures Customer Secures IaaS (e.g., EC2/VM) Hypervisor, physical hosts, network fabric OS patching, firewall rules, IAM, data, app PaaS (e.g., managed DB) OS, runtime, patching of platform Access control, data, schema, query security SaaS (e.g., email/CRM) Almost everything infrastructure- side User access, data classification, config settings IAM mechanics Cloud IAM is policy-based, not just user/group like on-prem AD. A policy is a JSON document specifying an Effect (Allow/Deny), an Action (e.g., s3:GetObject), a Resource (specific ARN or path), and often a Condition (source IP, MFA present, time window). Policies attach to identities (users, groups, roles) or to resources (bucket policies, key policies). Roles are the critical concept: instead of giving a VM or application long-lived credentials, you attach a role that issues short-lived, auto-rotating temporary tokens — this is how modern cloud workloads authenticate without embedding secrets in code.
At rest: data encrypted on disk/storage using provider-managed keys (SSE) or customer-managed keys (CMK/KMS) for stricter control and audit trail
In transit: TLS between every client-service and service-service hop, enforced via policy (deny non- HTTPS)

Key management: a dedicated KMS separates key custody from data custody — even a cloud admin with full storage access can't read data without a separate key-use permission Posture management (CSPM) Cloud Security Posture Management tools continuously scan your account/subscription against benchmarks (like CIS Benchmarks) and flag drift — a bucket that became public, a security group opened to 0.0.0.0/0, an IAM user with unused admin rights. This is the cloud-native evolution of the hardening and vulnerability management work from Sessions 96-97.
workflow: At FundedNext, if the CEx or infra team provisioned a cloud resource (say, a log storage bucket for CEx Pulse exports, or a VM hosting an internal tool), the practical security workflow would look like this:

1. Define the resource with least-privilege defaults: private by default, no public access, encryption enabled at creation, not bolted on later 2. Create a dedicated IAM role scoped to only the actions that resource needs (e.g., write-only for a logging service, not full admin) 3. Tag the resource with owner, environment (prod/staging), and data classification (e.g., contains-PII:

yes/no) so posture tools and audits can find it 4. Enable resource-level logging (access logs, API call logs) routed to a central log sink 5. Register the resource in the CSPM baseline so any future drift (e.g., someone flips it to public) triggers an alert 6. Periodic access review — quarterly check of who/what still has access, removing stale roles and unused keys This mirrors how you already think about AgentPlatform's domain-restricted auth and role-based permission tiers — cloud IAM is the same philosophy, expressed as provider-native policy documents instead of a Google Sheet permission column.
enterprise: Cloud Security sits at the intersection of three enterprise functions: Infrastructure/Cloud engineering (who provisions resources), Security/SecOps (who defines and monitors policy), and Compliance (who proves to regulators and auditors that controls exist). In a fintech like FundedNext, this triad is non-negotiable — prop trading platforms are frequently subject to financial-sector data protection expectations even without being a licensed bank, because payment processing and KYC data are involved.

Organizationally, Cloud Security responsibilities are usually split: a central cloud/platform team owns account structure, guardrails, and IAM policy templates; individual engineering teams own resource-level configuration within those guardrails; and a security team owns continuous monitoring, incident response, and audit evidence. This is the cloud equivalent of the SIEM/SOAR centralization you studied in Sessions 92-93 — detection is centralized even though provisioning is federated.

security: This session IS the security layer for cloud, but it's worth naming the specific attack patterns and controls that matter most in practice:
Public storage buckets/containers left open by default misconfiguration
Leaked long-lived access keys in source code, CI logs, or public repos
Overly broad IAM policies (wildcard * actions/resources) granted 'to make it work' and never tightened
Metadata service abuse (SSRF attacks that steal a VM's temporary role credentials via its instance metadata endpoint)
Unmonitored root/owner account — the single most powerful identity in an account, often without MFA enforced
Cross-account trust misconfiguration allowing unintended third parties to assume roles into your account Core controls
MFA enforced on all human identities, especially root/owner and admin roles
Least privilege IAM — start with zero permissions, add only what's proven necessary
No long-lived keys where a role/temporary credential is possible
Encryption by default, with customer-managed keys for sensitive data classes (KYC docs, payout records)
Network segmentation — private subnets for anything that doesn't need direct internet exposure
Continuous posture scanning (CSPM) plus alerting routed into the same SIEM used for on-prem security
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Diagnostic Step Access denied on a resource that should work IAM policy too narrow, or missing trust relationship on the role Check IAM policy simulator / access analyzer for the identity Application can't authenticate after key rotation Long-lived key rotated but not updated in app config Check for hardcoded keys vs. role- based auth in the app Data suddenly publicly accessible Bucket/container ACL or policy changed, often by automation or a broad IAM grant Review recent API/audit logs for policy change events Alerts firing for 'unusual API activity' Compromised key or role being used from unfamiliar location/service Cross-reference source IP/user- agent against known CI/CD or admin ranges Cost spike with no feature change Compromised credentials used for cryptomining or resource abuse Check for unexpected compute instances/regions never used before The single most useful troubleshooting habit in cloud security is treating the audit log (CloudTrail- equivalent) as ground truth before trusting the console UI — the console shows current state, the audit log shows how it got that way, which is what you actually need to diagnose a security incident.
example: A widely cited pattern across multiple public breach post-mortems (Capital One 2019, various exposed- bucket incidents reported by security researchers) follows a similar chain: a web application firewall or reverse proxy misconfiguration allowed a request to reach the cloud instance metadata service; the attacker retrieved the temporary IAM role credentials attached to that instance; those credentials had broader storage permissions than the application actually needed; the attacker used them to enumerate and exfiltrate data from storage buckets containing customer records.

I'm not fully certain of every technical detail of any single named incident, and you should verify specifics from an official source (e.g., the affected company's public breach disclosure or a regulator's report) rather than relying on my summary — the pattern itself, however, recurs constantly across cloud breach reports: over-permissioned role + exposed credential path + insufficient monitoring. The fix pattern is consistent too: scope IAM roles to least privilege, disable/restrict metadata service access from untrusted request paths, and alert on unusual data access volume.

automation: Cloud security scales only through automation — no team manually reviews every IAM policy change across thousands of resources. This connects directly to your PowerShell track and upcoming Layer 7 Automation sessions.

Example: PowerShell posture check pattern # Conceptual pattern - actual cmdlets vary by cloud provider module $publicResources = Get-CloudStorageResource | Where-Object { $_.PublicAccess -eq $true -and $_.Tags['env'] -eq 'prod' } if ($publicResources.Count -gt 0) { $publicResources | Export-Csv -Path .\posture_violations.csv - NoTypeInformation Send-AlertToTeam -Channel 'cex-infra-alerts' -Message "$ ($publicResources.Count) public prod resources found" } The pattern — query, filter against a policy rule, alert or auto-remediate — is the same automation shape you already use for AgentPlatform's date/time parsing fixes and CEx Pulse verification workflows, just pointed at cloud configuration state instead of Google Sheets rows.

misconceptions: "The cloud provider secures my data" — false; the provider secures the infrastructure, you secure your configuration and data, per the Shared Responsibility Model
"Private by default means secure" — many resources default to more open than people assume;
"IAM is just usernames and passwords" — modern cloud IAM is policy-based authorization with conditions, far closer to ACLs (Session 38) than to simple login credentials
"A VPN makes cloud workloads secure" — network-level access controls (Session 45) are one layer; they don't substitute for IAM, encryption, or monitoring
"Compliance certification means we're secure" — certifications (like SOC 2, ISO 27001) prove a process exists and was audited; they don't guarantee no misconfiguration exists today
anchors: Shared Responsibility = provider secures OF the cloud, you secure IN the cloud
Role > long-lived key, always, when the option exists
Audit log is ground truth; console is just current state
Public-by-mistake is the #1 real-world cloud breach cause — not exotic zero-days
CSPM is to cloud what vulnerability scanning (Session 97) was to on-prem hardening
connections: Cloud Security is the direct cloud-native descendant of nearly everything in Layer 6. Zero Trust (87) becomes 'never trust a request just because it's inside the VPC.' Firewalls (88) become security groups and network ACLs. IDS/IPS (89-90) become cloud-native threat detection services. EDR (91) becomes workload protection agents on cloud VMs/containers. SIEM (92) is where cloud audit logs land alongside on-prem logs for unified detection. SOAR (93) automates the remediation — auto-revoking a leaked key the moment it's detected.

It also reaches back further: PKI/Certificates (61-62) underpin every TLS connection and every KMS key. Kerberos/NTLM/LDAP (53-55) conceptually map to how cloud identity federation works when a Gulf enterprise bridges its on-prem Active Directory into Azure AD/Entra ID or AWS IAM Identity Center — a very common real-world hybrid setup you're likely to encounter. And it sets up everything still coming in Layer 9 (Monitoring, Serverless, Containers, Automation) and Layer 10's architecture- level Security and Compliance sessions.

lab: This lab is designed to run against a free-tier cloud account (AWS, Azure, or GCP — pick whichever you're most likely to need for your Gulf job search) and takes roughly 60-90 minutes. Mandatory hands- on, not optional reading — same standard as your Subnetting lab.

7. Create a free-tier account if you don't have one; enable MFA on the root/owner identity immediately, before doing anything else 8. Create a non-root IAM user or role for yourself with a custom policy granting only storage read/write on one specific bucket/container — not admin 9. Create that one storage resource, leave it fully private, and enable server-side encryption 10. Attempt to make the resource public through the console UI and observe what warning/guardrail the provider shows you — screenshot it for your notes 11. Revert to private, then check the audit/activity log for the account and find the exact log entry recording your public-access change 12. Write a short CSPM-style rule in plain English (e.g., 'flag any storage resource where PublicAccess = true') and identify which native provider service would enforce it automatically 13. Delete all created resources when done to avoid any charges
